title: How Do You Read Ancient Charred Scrolls? Make Your Own - Nautilus
gist: A new technique could help read the Herculaneum scrolls, more than 1,800 papyri carbonized by the 79 CE eruption of Mount Vesuvius; earlier attempts to unroll them physically destroyed many scrolls.

insights.claim: The 79 CE eruption of Mount Vesuvius turned more than 1,800 Greek and Roman papyrus scrolls in a Herculaneum library to charcoal, which preserved them while making them unreadable.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: This is a large archive of unread ancient text, and non-destructive imaging and AI decoding approaches are competing to read it.
insights.locator: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE

insights.claim: Eighteenth-century efforts to unroll the carbonized scrolls physically were extremely slow: one scroll took four years at a few millimeters a day. Many scrolls were destroyed, and Italian officials halted the work.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Past physical methods failed, which is why non-invasive reading technologies matter here.

insights.claim: Making replica charred scrolls is presented as a new technique that could help unlock the Herculaneum scrolls.
